title: Disjoint set union
sub: Union-Find: Number of Provinces, Redundant Connection and Kruskal — connectivity as edges arrive, in almost O(1)
cards/0/body:
Number of Provinces (LeetCode #547). Up to 200 cities and an n×n matrix isConnected: 1 means two cities are joined by a road. A province is a group of cities connected directly or through others. How many provinces are there? That's the number of connected components, and the DFS from lesson 1 solves it in O(n²) over the matrix.

Now make it online: edges arrive one at a time, and after each one you're asked “are a and b connected?” or “how many components are there now?”. A BFS per question is O(V + E); for 10⁵ edges and questions that's 10¹⁰. You need a structure that merges groups and answers “same group?” almost instantly.

Disjoint set union (Union-Find, DSU) is a forest: each group is a tree, its root is the group's representative, parent[x] is x's parent, and a root has parent[x] == x. Find(x) climbs to the root. Union(a, b) hangs the root of one tree under the root of the other. a and b are connected ⇔ Find(a) == Find(b). No adjacency lists, no traversal: just an int[n] array.
cards/1/title: Two improvements: by size and path compression
cards/1/body:
The naive version degenerates: if a big tree keeps getting hung under a single vertex, trees turn into chains, and Find costs O(n).

Union by size: hang the smaller tree under the root of the larger one. A vertex's depth grows only when its tree merges into one at least as large — that is, the size of its group at least doubles. That can happen at most log₂ n times: the height is ≤ log₂ n. (Union “by rank” stores an estimate of height instead of size — same properties.)

Path compression: while Find climbs, it re-hangs vertices closer to the root. A simple version is “skip one”: parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]. The next Find along this path is shorter.

Each improvement on its own gives O(log n). Together — O(α(n)) amortized per operation, where α is the inverse Ackermann function: for any n that fits in memory, α(n) ≤ 4. In practice, a constant. Union returns a bool: false means “already in the same group” — it'll come in handy.
cards/2/q: The naive Union-Find from the first card: parent[Find(a)] = Find(b). We call Union(0, i) for i = 1, 2, …, n − 1 with n = 10⁵. Roughly how much work is that?
cards/2/options/0: ≈ 5·10⁹: the tree is a chain 0 → 1 → 2 → …, and Find(0) walks all of it every time
cards/2/options/1: ≈ 10⁵: each Union is a single assignment
cards/2/options/2: ≈ 1.7·10⁶: the tree's height is at most log₂ n
cards/2/explain: Union(0, 1) sets parent[0] = 1, Union(0, 2) sets parent[1] = 2: the root of zero's group goes under the new vertex every time, and the path from 0 to the root grows by 1. At step i, Find(0) walks i links — n²/2 ≈ 5·10⁹ in total. With union by size, the single vertex i goes under the big root, and Find(0) is one or two steps.
cards/2/wrong/1: There is one assignment, but two Finds come before it, and Find(0) climbs the whole chain, which grows with every call.
cards/2/wrong/2: log₂ n is the bound for union by size. Here size is ignored, and the height reaches n − 1.
cards/3/explain: “Skip one” compression: a vertex is re-hung on its grandparent. Equal roots mean one group already, so Union changes nothing and honestly returns false. After the swap ra is the root of the larger tree; the root rb goes under it, not the vertex b itself. The new group's size is the sum of both sizes, not +1.
cards/4/title: Number of Provinces and Redundant Connection
cards/4/body:
#547: create a Dsu for n cities and call Union for every pair i < j with isConnected[i][j] == 1. Every successful merge lowers Count by 1 — the answer is dsu.Count. O(n²·α(n)).

Redundant Connection (LeetCode #684). A tree of n vertices (3 ≤ n ≤ 1000, numbered from 1) plus one extra edge — n edges in all. Return an edge whose removal leaves a tree; if several fit, the one that comes last in the list.

Walk the edges and call Union. false means the endpoints are already connected by another path, so this edge closes a cycle. There is one cycle, and any of its edges could be removed. The first false comes from the cycle edge that appears latest in the list: until it arrives, the cycle isn't closed. That's exactly the required answer. O(n·α(n)), with no traversal and no adjacency lists.
cards/5/q: Redundant Connection on [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4],[1,4],[1,5]] with the Dsu class (by size, with compression). What is in parent after the first three Unions, and what happens on the edge [1,4]?
cards/5/options/0: 2, 3 and 4 point to 1 — a star; Union(1, 4) returns false, the answer is [1,4]
cards/5/options/1: A chain 4 → 3 → 2 → 1; Union(1, 4) returns false, the answer is [1,4]
cards/5/options/2: 2, 3 and 4 point to 1; Union(1, 4) returns true, the answer is [1,5]
cards/5/explain: Union(1, 2): equal sizes, no swap — parent[2] = 1. Union(2, 3): Find(2) = 1, group 1 is larger than the single 3 — parent[3] = 1. Likewise parent[4] = 1. Everyone hangs directly on the root: union by size keeps the tree from stretching. On [1,4] both Finds give 1 — false, and that's the answer: the edge [1,5] doesn't close a cycle.
cards/5/wrong/1: The naive version would give a chain. Here a single vertex always goes under the root of the larger group, so the tree is a star of height 1.
cards/5/wrong/2: Find(1) and Find(4) are both 1: the endpoints are already in one group, so Union returns false. [1,5] attaches the new vertex 5 and creates no cycle.
cards/6/q: #684 on [[1,2],[1,3],[2,3]]: this code returns an empty array instead of [2,3]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/6/explain: It must hang the root, not the vertex itself. Union(1, 2): parent[1] = 2. Union(1, 3): Find(1) = 2, but the code writes parent[1] = 3 — so 1 leaves 2, and 2 stays a separate root. On [2,3], Find(2) = 2 and Find(3) = 3 — “different groups”, Union returns true, and the redundant edge is never found. It needs parent[ra] = rb.
cards/7/body:
The graph is given in full and never changes — components can be counted by DFS/BFS or by Union-Find, both O(V + E). Union-Find is handy because no adjacency lists are needed: edges in any order, one pass, O(V) memory.

Edges are added along the way, with questions in between — Union-Find: each operation is almost O(1), while a traversal would have to be repeated. Example: Number of Islands II (#305): land appears one cell at a time, and after each you need the number of islands. A vertex is the cell r·w + c; new land means Count++ and a Union with neighboring land.

What Union-Find can't do: delete edges or split groups, find paths and distances, respect edge direction. If walls are both built and destroyed, region labels are recomputed with a traversal (lesson 1).

Edges in increasing weight order — “at what moment did a and b first end up together”. Minimum spanning trees (next) and minimax paths (u12.l2) are built on this.

In a game. A destructible level: a wall between rooms is destroyed — Union; “are the bases connected” — compare two Finds. Caves after a cellular automaton: the regions from labeling (lesson 1) are vertices, and corridors are dug until Count reaches 1.
cards/7/deep:
Offline deletions. If all queries are known in advance, edge deletions can be reversed: walk the queries from the end, and a deletion becomes an addition. That's how “edges disappear, how many components after each step” problems are solved.

Recursive Find. The short form parent[x] = Find(parent[x]) compresses the path fully, but it is recursive. With union by size the depth is at most log₂ n, so the stack is safe. Without it, a chain of 10⁵ vertices means 10⁵ frames, and a recursive Find crashes exactly where the recursive traversal from lesson 1 does. The iterative “skip one” version is always safe.

Union-Find with data. The root is a convenient place for group data: size, sum, minimum, a member list. When merging, the smaller group flows into the larger — the same “smaller under larger” principle: each element moves at most log₂ n times, so member lists merge in O(n log n) total.

Jobs and Burst. Union-Find is two int arrays, that is, a NativeArray<int> with no references and no garbage. Merging groups from several threads at once isn't straightforward — the root write would have to be atomic; a single-threaded Burst job is usually enough.
cards/8/q: A destructible map: the player breaks walls between rooms, and after each destruction the game checks whether the two teams' bases are connected. Walls are never rebuilt. What do you do?
cards/8/options/0: Union-Find over rooms: a wall breaks — Union; the check is Find(baseA) == Find(baseB)
cards/8/options/1: A BFS from base A after each destruction: it stops as soon as it finds base B
cards/8/options/2: Kruskal by wall strength: the minimum spanning tree shows which bases are connected
cards/8/options/3: Union-Find, and if walls start being rebuilt, call Union in reverse
cards/8/explain: Edges are only added and questions come in between — exactly the Union-Find case: each event and each check is almost O(1). BFS gives a correct answer too, but at O(rooms + walls) per event.
cards/8/wrong/1: While the bases aren't connected, BFS walks the whole component of base A — over and over, after every broken wall.
cards/8/wrong/2: A spanning tree answers “how to connect everything most cheaply”, while here you need the current connectivity after each event.
cards/8/wrong/3: There is no reverse Union: the structure doesn't remember which edge merged the groups and can't split a tree. If walls are rebuilt, connectivity is recomputed with a traversal.
cards/9/body:
Min Cost to Connect All Points (LeetCode #1584). Up to 1000 points on a plane, an edge costs the Manhattan distance |x₁ − x₂| + |y₁ − y₂|. Connect all the points with the minimum total cost. That's the minimum spanning tree: n − 1 edges, all vertices connected, the smallest sum of weights.

Kruskal's algorithm: sort all edges by weight and go from light to heavy; take an edge if Union returns true — it joins two different groups. An edge inside one group would form a cycle — skip it. Stop when one group is left.

Why it's correct: the lightest edge between two groups can always be part of some minimum spanning tree. If a tree did without it, add it — a cycle appears, the cycle has another edge between the same groups that is no lighter — remove that one, and the sum doesn't grow.

Cost. The graph is complete: n(n − 1)/2 ≈ 5·10⁵ edges, sorting is O(E log E) ≈ 10⁷ — it passes.

Unity: a dungeon. Rooms are points, possible corridors are edges with a length. The spanning tree connects every room with the smallest total corridor length, but it's a tree — all dead ends. So after Kruskal some rejected edges are added back, say every tenth one, to create loops.
cards/9/deep:
Prim versus Kruskal. A complete graph has Θ(n²) edges, and Kruskal spends O(n² log n) time and O(n²) memory on their list. Prim without a heap — an array “distance to the tree” over n vertices; at each step pick the closest and update the rest — is O(n²) time and O(n) memory. For #1584 it's faster and doesn't hold 5·10⁵ tuples. Kruskal wins on sparse graphs, where E ≈ V.

Fewer edges. For Euclidean distance the minimum spanning tree always lies within the Delaunay triangulation, which has about 3n edges instead of n²/2. That's why dungeon generators usually triangulate the room centers, build the tree on that, and then add back a few edges for loops.

Overflow. In #1584 coordinates are up to 10⁶ in absolute value: one edge is up to 4·10⁶, and under these constraints the tree's total fits in an int. With larger weights or more points, sum in a long.

Sorting tuples. ValueTuple compares fields left to right, which is why the weight goes first. List.Sort is an introspective sort and isn't stable; for a spanning tree that doesn't matter: with equal weights any order works, and the sum is the same.
cards/10/q: Points [[0,0],[2,2],[3,10],[5,2],[7,0]], numbered 0–4. The lightest edges: 1–3 (3), 0–1 (4), 3–4 (4), 0–3 (7), 0–4 (7), 1–4 (7), 1–2 (9). Which edge does Kruskal skip first, and why?
cards/10/options/0: 0–3 (7): after 1–3 and 0–1, vertices 0 and 3 are already in one group
cards/10/explain: Take 1–3, 0–1 and 3–4: each joins different groups, the sum is 11, the group is {0, 1, 3, 4}. The edge 0–3 is inside the group: Union returns false, skip it; the same for 0–4 and 1–4. 1–2 attaches point 2: the sum is 20, one group — done. The answer for these points is 20.
cards/10/wrong/1: A vertex's degree doesn't matter: 3–4 joins the group {1, 3} with the single vertex 4 — a new connection, so the edge is taken.
cards/10/wrong/2: 1–2 is the only way to point 2 among those listed, and Union returns true for it. What gets skipped isn't heavy edges but edges inside a group.
cards/11/q: You are solving Redundant Connection out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/11/items/0: Clarify: vertices from 1, exactly n edges, if several fit return the last one
cards/11/items/1: Observation: a tree plus one edge has exactly one cycle; the extra edge closes it
cards/11/items/2: Idea: Union-Find over the edges in list order; the first Union that returns false is the answer
cards/11/items/3: Code: a Dsu with union by size and path compression, Union returns a bool
cards/11/items/4: Run [[1,2],[1,3],[2,3]]: on [2,3] both Finds give the same root
cards/11/items/5: Complexity: O(n·α(n)) — almost linear, O(n) memory
cards/11/items/6: Why the first false is exactly the cycle's last edge in the list
cards/11/explain: After clarifying comes the property “tree + edge = one cycle”, then the idea, the code and the run. The proof that the first false matches “last in the list” finishes the answer: it's usually asked.
cards/12/q: Match the problem to the technique.
cards/12/pairs/1/0: The redundant edge in a tree
cards/12/pairs/1/1: The first Union that returns false
cards/12/pairs/2/0: Islands appear one cell at a time
cards/12/pairs/3/0: Connect all points as cheaply as possible
cards/12/pairs/4/0: Walls are both destroyed and built
cards/12/pairs/5/0: Find without degenerating into a chain
